text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:

- German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel expects "substantial results" from next week's EU summit in Amsterdam, with all national governments essentially seeking an accord despite their many differences.
- Further German government coalition talks on Wednesday morning failed to bring the various parties any closer to an agreement on a dispute over how to plug budget holes.
- The business affairs council of the Christian Democrats demands new state cost-savings measures that would bring in 125 billion marks by the year 2000.
- For the first time since unification in 1990, Germany's birth rate increased last year, according to official statistics.

- Bonn and Paris seek to settle differences over Europe's currency union, with the German government ready to end its opposition to an employment chapter in the EU treaty and France prepared to ratify the stability pact on post-EMU currency stability.
- Bonn set to ban mobile telephones, laptops and other electronic devices onboard aircraft.
- Bavarian politicians says Germany should not sign the so-called Maastricht II updated EU treaty without a number of reforms, particularly on immigration.

- The government coalition is seeking to water down plans contained within its proposed tax reform to slash a number of tax-breaks currently available to employees. In return, employers are to be asked to contribute more to the reform, which seeks overall to cut taxes.
- Bonn and Paris agree in principle on the nature of reforms to the EU treaty that will be discussed at next week's Amsterdam summit.
- Multimedia providers will according to a new law be banned from passing on information about their clients to credit-checking agencies.
Hannover-based Preussag announces plans to takeover the majority of the Hamburg-based logistics and transportation group Hapag-Lloyd.

- Government and opposition parties agree the euro must be introduced on time as planned in 1999, but fundamental differences exist how job policies can or should be anchored into the new Maastricht II treaty.
- A court in Kiel sentences those convicted of sinking the "Lucona" freighter some 20 years ago in one of the world's largest cases of insurance fraud to 14 years jail.
